children.children: What is the difference between a population and a sample?

children: is every member of the group you care about, such as every bulb a factory will ever make. A

children.children: In a perfect world, a data scientist would possess "God's View" access to every single data point, past, present, and future. If you wanted to know the average height of humans, you would instantly measure all 8 billion people. If you wanted to know if a user clicks an ad, you would simulate every possible user in existence.

children: In reality, we are constrained by time, cost, and physics. We cannot measure everything. We must rely on a subset of reality to understand the whole. This is the core conflict of statistics:

children.className: bg-muted/50 border-l-4 border-amber-300 dark:border-amber-500 p-6 mb-6 rounded-r-lg

children: The entire pot of soup. To know the
flavor profile perfectly, you would need to drink the entire pot (which destroys the product).
If the spoonful is salty, you assume the whole pot is salty.
But what if you didn't stir the pot? Your spoonful might be bland while the bottom is pure salt. This problem is called

children.children: The entire set of all elements (individuals, objects, events) that are of interest for a specific study. It is the "ground truth."

children: All pixels in an image, all transactions in a bank's history, every human on Earth.

children.children: A subset of the population selected for analysis. We collect data from the sample to estimate truths about the population.

children: A 224x224 crop of an image, the last 1000 transactions, a survey of 500 people.

children.children: In interviews and literature, the notation tells you immediately if we are discussing the theoretical truth (Population) or the calculated estimate (Sample).

/ml-math/statistics/hypothesis-testing.subtitle: The mathematical framework for distinguishing signal from noise.

children.children: Hypothesis testing is the statistical method for making decisions under uncertainty. It takes two opposing ideas about a population and uses sample data to decide which is more likely true.

children.className: bg-muted/50 border-l-4 border-emerald-300 dark:border-emerald-500 p-6 mb-6 rounded-r-lg

children.children: In Data Science, we constantly see patterns. "Model A has 85% accuracy, Model B has 86%." Is Model B actually better? Or was that 1% difference just random luck?
Hypothesis testing gives us a mathematical "Yes" or "No" (with a probability attached) to that question.

For example, if a company claims their website gets 50 visitors a day on average, we use hypothesis testing to analyze past visitor data. We determine if the actual average is indeed 50, or if the deviation we see in our sample is significant enough to prove them wrong.
The logic of hypothesis testing parallels a criminal trial. This analogy helps clarify why we phrase things as "Fail to reject" rather than "Accept."

children.children: ANOVA, or analysis of variance, tests whether the means of three or more groups differ by comparing the variation between the group means with the variation within each group. When the ratio of the two, the F-statistic, is large, at least one group mean is likely different, and a single ANOVA avoids the extra false positives that many pairwise t-tests would produce.
A/B testing (T-test) is great for comparing two things (Control vs Variant). But what if you have 3 landing pages? Or 4 different ML models? Or 5 different light bulb filament types?

What is the difference between Pearson and Spearman correlation?

Pearson correlation measures how closely two variables follow a straight line, using their raw values, while Spearman correlation measures how closely they follow any consistently increasing or decreasing trend, using their ranks. Use Pearson for roughly linear data without large outliers, and Spearman for curved but monotonic relationships, ordinal data or data with outliers.

/ml-math/statistics/bayesian-frequentist.subtitle: Two philosophies of probability, one fundamental question: What does "probability" even mean?

children.children: What is the difference between Bayesian and frequentist statistics?

Frequentist statistics treats a parameter as a fixed but unknown value and judges methods by how they behave over many repeated samples, using p-values and confidence intervals. Bayesian statistics treats the parameter as uncertain, combines a prior belief with the data to get a posterior distribution, and reports credible intervals.

children.children: What is the law of large numbers?

Flip a fair coin ten times and you may see 70% heads; flip it ten thousand times and the share of heads will be very close to 50%. children.children: What is the difference between the weak and strong law of large numbers?

The weak law says that, for a large enough sample, the average is very likely to be close to the true mean; the strong law says that the sequence of averages actually converges to the true mean with probability 1. The strong law is the stronger guarantee, because it describes the whole sequence rather than one sample size at a time.

What is the difference between the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem?

The law of large numbers tells you where the sample mean ends up, which is at the true mean, while the central limit theorem tells you how the sample mean is spread around that value for a finite sample, which is approximately a normal distribution whose width shrinks like one over the square root of the sample size. SVD vs PCA: what is the difference?

SVD is a general matrix factorization that works on any matrix, while PCA is a specific dimensionality-reduction method that finds the directions of greatest variance in a dataset. In practice, PCA is usually computed with SVD: centring the data matrix and taking its SVD gives the principal components as the right singular vectors, without ever forming the covariance matrix. Eigendecomposition, by contrast, only applies to square matrices.

/ml-math/linear-algebra/pca.subtitle: Finding the most informative view of high-dimensional data. The workhorse of unsupervised dimensionality reduction.

children: reduces the number of features in a dataset by finding the directions along which the data varies most. Those directions are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix. Projecting the data onto the top few keeps most of the information in far fewer, uncorrelated features.

children.children: Real-world datasets are often high-dimensional. A customer might be described by 500 features: age, income, location, browsing history, purchase frequency, click patterns, and hundreds more. Many of these features are redundant or highly correlated (annual income and tax paid, for instance).

children: is an unsupervised technique that transforms a large set of correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables called
. These new variables are ordered: PC1 captures the most variance, PC2 captures the second most (while being orthogonal to PC1), and so on.

Proper preprocessing is critical for PCA to work correctly.
Subtract the mean from each feature. This ensures PCA finds directions of maximum variance around the data center, not around the origin.
Divide by standard deviation. Without scaling, features with larger units dominate. Exception: if all features are in the same units (e.g., all pixels), scaling may not be needed.

Images are extremely high-dimensional (100×100 = 10,000 pixels). PCA on a face dataset yields "eigenfaces," which are the principal components of facial variation. Any face can be reconstructed as a weighted sum of just a few hundred eigenfaces, enabling efficient storage and recognition.

Before training classifiers on high-dimensional data, apply PCA to reduce features from thousands to hundreds. This speeds up training, reduces overfitting, and often improves accuracy by removing noise.
To visualize clusters in 50D data, project to 2D using the top 2 PCs. While you lose information, the retained dimensions capture the most variance, often revealing cluster structure.
Project data to k PCs and reconstruct. Normal points reconstruct well; anomalies have high reconstruction error because they don't fit the learned patterns.

Stock returns are correlated. PCA extracts "market factors": PC1 is often the overall market (all stocks move together), PC2 might be sector rotation. Quants use these for risk modeling and portfolio optimization.

children.children: AUC-ROC is calculated by sorting the model's scores, sweeping the decision threshold to get a true positive rate and a false positive rate at each step, and integrating the resulting ROC curve, usually with the trapezoidal rule. Good News: Local Minima Are Often Good
Research shows that in over-parameterized networks, most local minima have loss values very close to the global minimum. Getting "stuck" in a local minimum isn't as catastrophic as feared.
Minima with small Hessian eigenvalues ("flat" regions) tend to generalize better than "sharp" minima. This is related to PAC-Bayesian theory and explains why SGD noise helps.
Having more parameters than needed creates many equivalent good solutions, making optimization easier. This is one reason why bigger models are often easier to train.
ResNets with skip connections create a smoother loss landscape with fewer saddle points. This is why very deep networks became trainable with residual connections.

/ml-math/optimization/convex-optimizatio.chapterTitle: Convex vs Non-Convex Optimization: What Changes for Gradient Descent

children: , every local minimum is a global minimum, so gradient descent with a small enough step size cannot settle in a worse valley. In

, the surface can contain several minima, saddle points and plateaus, so where you start can change where training ends. Linear and logistic regression are classic examples of convex problems, whereas training a neural network is a non-convex problem.

children.children: Formally, a convex optimization problem minimizes a convex function over a convex set, meaning a set where the straight line between any two of its points stays inside it. Most of this lesson is about unconstrained training losses, where the set is the whole parameter space and only the function matters.
What is the difference between convex and non-convex optimization?

The practical difference lies in what it means when training converges. On a convex loss, a point where the gradient is zero is a global minimum, so convergence means the problem is solved. On a non-convex loss, a zero-gradient point could be a minimum, a maximum or a saddle, and even a genuine minimum may not be the best one available.
A local minimum can be worse than the global one
Every one is a global minimum (for a differentiable loss)
Not for the minimum value. It can matter for which minimizer you reach
It can change the loss you end up with
Reaches the minimum value, at a known rate for smooth losses with a suitable step size
The gradient gets small. Nothing is promised about the quality of the point
Linear regression with squared error, logistic regression with cross-entropy, SVM with hinge loss

Two rows of this table are easy to misread, so each gets its own section below: convex does not mean there is only one answer (it means there is one minimum value), and non-convex does not mean gradient descent gets stuck (it means the guarantee is weaker). It also helps to remember that convexity is a property of the loss viewed as a function of the parameters, which is why the model, the loss and the optimizer are best treated as three separate choices.

Why are neural network losses non-convex?

The root cause is that a network's output multiplies parameters from different layers, and a product of parameters is not convex in those parameters. You can see this with a network that has only two weights.

children.children: This agrees with the theory. Lee et al. (2016) proved that for smooth functions whose saddle points all have a direction of negative curvature, gradient descent with a small enough step size converges to a saddle only from a set of starting points of measure zero, and the saddle in our toy model is exactly this kind of strict saddle.

For large networks, two results are worth knowing, and they make different kinds of claim. Kawaguchi (2016) proved that for deep linear networks with squared loss, the loss is non-convex but every local minimum is global and every other critical point is a saddle; his extension to nonlinear networks relies on an independence assumption. Dauphin et al. (2014) argued, using statistical physics, random matrix theory and experiments, that in high dimensions the main obstacle is saddle points and the plateaus around them rather than poor local minima, which is a well-supported argument rather than a theorem that holds for every model and dataset.

children: Together, these results explain why “stuck in a bad local minimum” is rarely the right first diagnosis when a run fails; the step size, the initialization and the gradient computation are better places to start looking. The lessons on

children.children: Do momentum and Adam make the problem convex?
No. An optimizer changes the path taken across the loss surface, but it has no effect on whether the objective itself is convex.

Mini-batch noise in SGD plays a role similar to the small offset in the last listing, since it can push an iterate off a saddle's stable direction, although this is an intuition for why noise helps rather than a proof.

children.children: None of these methods gives a global-optimality guarantee on a non-convex loss. When two optimizers end at different losses on the same network, the difference comes from the paths they took across one fixed surface. Adaptive methods often train faster in practice, but that is an empirical observation on particular problems rather than a theorem.
What mistakes do people make when reasoning about convexity?
Each of the beliefs below is almost right, which is exactly why it keeps coming up, so the more precise version follows each one.

children.className: text-muted-foreground leading-relaxed mb-6 space-y-3 list-disc pl-5

children.children: “Convex means there is only one minimum.”

children: Convexity means there is one minimum value, but the minimizers can form a line or a plane, as the duplicated-feature example showed.
It means the only guarantee is that the gradient gets small. Landing exactly on a saddle is rare, and the bigger risks are usually the step size, the initialization and plateaus.

children.children: “A zero gradient means I found the answer.”

children: That is true for a differentiable convex loss, but otherwise you need to check the Hessian eigenvalues to tell whether the point is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle.

children.children: “My model is convex because it is simple.”

children: Convexity is a property of the loss as a function of the parameters, which is why logistic regression is convex with cross-entropy but not with squared error.

children.children: “A larger learning rate just trains faster.”

children.children: What is the difference between batch, mini-batch and stochastic gradient descent?

Batch gradient descent computes each update from the whole training set, stochastic gradient descent uses a single example, and mini-batch gradient descent uses a small batch, usually between 32 and 512 examples. Mini-batch is the default in deep learning because its gradients are stable enough to converge while each step still uses the GPU efficiently.

children.children: What is the difference between momentum and Nesterov momentum?

Classical momentum adds a running average of past gradients to every step, which speeds up progress along consistent directions and damps oscillations across a ravine. Nesterov momentum evaluates the gradient at the point momentum is about to carry the parameters to, so it corrects course earlier and overshoots less.

children.children: Adam vs RMSprop vs AdaGrad: what is the difference?

children: All three give every parameter its own learning rate by dividing by the size of its recent gradients.
divides by the sum of all past squared gradients, so its learning rate only ever shrinks;
uses a moving average instead, so the rate can recover; and
adds momentum on top of RMSprop and corrects both averages for their start-up bias, which is why it is the usual default.

Consider training a word embedding model. The word "the" appears millions of times; its gradient is massive and stable. The word "serendipity" appears twice; its gradient is tiny and unreliable.

The test set's loss surface is shifted slightly from the training one, so a wide valley still has low loss after that shift while a narrow ravine can climb steeply. Keskar et al. children.children: What is the difference between L1 and L2 regularization?

L1 regularization adds the sum of the absolute weights to the loss, which drives many weights to exactly zero and gives a sparse model that effectively selects features. L2 regularization adds the sum of the squared weights, which shrinks every weight smoothly towards zero without removing any and copes better with correlated features.

/ml-math/optimization/batch-normalizatio.subtitle: One of the most important innovations in deep learning. Normalizes layer inputs to accelerate training and improve generalization.

children.children: Batch normalization standardizes each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then rescales it with two learned parameters, gamma and beta. It lets deep networks train with higher learning rates and makes them less sensitive to initialization, and at inference time it switches to running averages collected during training.

children: Batch Normalization (BN), introduced by Ioffe and Szegedy (2015), revolutionized deep learning training. Before BN, training very deep networks was notoriously difficult: gradients would vanish or explode during

children.children: BN solves this by normalizing the inputs to each layer, making training faster, more stable, and less sensitive to initialization. It's now a standard component in most modern architectures.

/ml-math/graph-theory/graph-representati.subtitle: How you store a graph in memory determines what operations are fast, what is slow, and how much space you need. Choose wisely.

A graph is an abstract concept: a set of nodes connected by edges. But computers do not understand abstract concepts. They understand memory addresses, arrays, and pointers. Before you can run any graph algorithm, you must first answer a fundamental question:

children.children: how do I store this graph in memory?

The answer is not straightforward. Different representations make different operations efficient. Choosing the wrong one can turn an O(1) lookup into O(n), or balloon your memory usage from O(n) to O(n²). This is especially critical in machine learning, where graphs can have millions of nodes.

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children.children: There is no universally "best" representation. Adjacency matrices excel at checking if two nodes are connected. Adjacency lists are superior for iterating over neighbors. Edge lists are compact for sparse graphs. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for writing efficient graph algorithms.

/ml-math/graph-theory/spectral-graph.subtitle: How eigenvalues reveal hidden graph structure. The mathematical foundation behind clustering, community detection, and modern GNNs.

children: studies a graph through the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix built from it, usually the graph Laplacian

. The number of zero eigenvalues counts connected components, the second-smallest eigenvalue measures how well connected the graph is, and its eigenvector, the Fiedler vector, splits the graph into clusters.
The graphs studied here are data graphs, such as social networks, molecules or citation networks. They are different from the
that record the operations of a model for backpropagation, although both are made of nodes and edges.

children.children: Graphs are combinatorial objects: nodes and edges. Linear algebra deals with matrices and vector spaces. At first glance, these seem like separate worlds. Spectral graph theory is the bridge between them.

children: The core insight is simple yet profound:
we can represent a graph as a matrix, then analyze that matrix using

. The "spectrum" of a graph (its set of eigenvalues) encodes structural information that is invisible to the naked eye: how clustered the graph is, whether it is connected, how information flows through it.

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children: Eigenvalues are to graphs what frequencies are to sound waves. A chord sounds different from a single note because it has multiple frequencies. Similarly, a clustered graph "sounds different" from a random graph because its eigenvalue spectrum has a different shape.
The term "spectral" comes from physics. When you shine white light through a prism, it splits into a spectrum of colors, each color corresponding to a different frequency. In linear algebra, the

children.children: Just as the color spectrum tells you about light's composition, a matrix's spectrum tells you about its fundamental properties. For graphs, this means the eigenvalue spectrum reveals:
How many connected components? Is the graph well-connected or fragile?
Are there natural communities? How separable are they?
How quickly does information spread? Are there bottlenecks?
Can nodes be split into two groups with edges only between groups?

The smallest eigenvalue is always 0, with eigenvector

children.children: The second smallest eigenvalue is arguably the most important. It measures how well-connected the graph is:
λ₂ = 0 means graph is disconnected (multiple components)
λ₂ small means graph is "almost disconnected" (has bottlenecks)

children.children: Step through the spectral clustering algorithm to see how matrix operations reveal graph structure.
Spectral clustering extends the Fiedler vector idea to k clusters:
Compute L = D - A (or use a normalized variant for better results).
Find the k smallest eigenvectors of L: v₁, v₂, ..., vₖ.
Create an n × k matrix U where row i is [v₁[i], v₂[i], ..., vₖ[i]]. Each node is now a point in k-dimensional space.
Apply standard k-means clustering to the rows of U. The cluster labels transfer back to the original nodes.

children: The spectral embedding "untangles" the graph structure. In the original graph, clusters may be interleaved in complex ways. In the spectral embedding, clusters become well-separated Gaussian-like blobs that k-means can easily identify.

/ml-math/graph-theory/random-walks.subtitle: From Google's PageRank to modern graph embeddings: how random exploration reveals graph structure.

children.children: What is a random walk on a graph?

A random walk on a graph starts at a node and repeatedly moves to a randomly chosen neighbour, with the probability of each move given by a transition matrix. After many steps the walk settles into a stationary distribution, which is the idea behind PageRank, and short walks are how node2vec and DeepWalk learn node embeddings.

children: Imagine placing a particle on a node in a
and letting it wander randomly from node to node, following edges. Where will it end up after many steps? Which nodes will it visit most frequently?

, turns out to be extraordinarily powerful. It is the foundation of Google's PageRank algorithm, modern graph embedding methods like node2vec and DeepWalk, sampling algorithms for large graphs, and the theory of Markov chains.

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children: view of graphs. Instead of asking "what is the shortest path?", we ask "how likely is the walker to reach this node?" This perspective reveals global structure that local analysis misses.

/ml-math/graph-theory/computational-grap.subtitle: The fundamental architecture that powers modern deep learning systems.

children: is a directed acyclic graph in which each node is an operation, such as an addition or a matrix multiply, and each edge carries a value from one operation to the next. Deep learning frameworks build this graph during the forward pass and then walk it backwards, applying the
at every node, which is how

children.children: In a perfect world, training a neural network would be instantaneous. Every computation would happen simultaneously, gradients would flow backwards effortlessly, and we would have infinite computational resources. Reality, however, demands a more elegant solution.

children: come in. They are the fundamental data structure that modern deep learning frameworks use to organize, optimize, and execute the complex web of calculations required to train neural networks. Understanding them is key to understanding how frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch actually work under the hood.

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children.children: Computational graphs are not just implementation details: they fundamentally shape how we can train and deploy models. They enable automatic differentiation, distributed training, and efficient memory management.
How do graphs represent a computation?
A computational graph is a directed graph where:
Represent operations (addition, multiplication, activation functions) or variables
Represent the flow of data (tensors, scalars, gradients) between operations
Determine execution order: a node cannot execute until all its parent nodes complete

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg mb-6

children.children: Computations do not always need to happen sequentially. Some operations are independent and can run in parallel. A computational graph automatically identifies these opportunities, managing dependencies and parallelizing execution across threads or distributed systems.

Think of it like a recipe. Some steps must happen in order (you cannot bake before mixing), but others can happen simultaneously (chopping vegetables while water boils). The graph structure encodes these dependencies naturally.

Each node in a computational graph operates like a miniature processing unit. Understanding what happens inside a node helps explain how the entire graph coordinates execution.
The node monitors its parent nodes, waiting for all required resources (data, gradients, or execution signals) to become available.
Once all parent resources arrive, the node performs its computation. This might be a matrix multiplication, applying an activation function, or any mathematical operation.
After computation completes, the node makes its output available to its child nodes, signaling them to check if they are ready to execute.

children: In concurrent programming terms, you can think of each node as a critical section that acquires locks on parent resources before executing. This design elegantly handles both
: directed graphs with no cycles. This seemingly simple constraint provides powerful guarantees:

children.children: Without cycles, nodes never wait in circular dependencies
There is always a valid execution order
Gradients flow backwards through the graph unambiguously
All nodes at the same "level" can execute simultaneously

While it is technically possible to have cycles in computational graphs (recurrent neural networks use them), most frameworks "unroll" these cycles into DAGs for a fixed number of time steps during training.

/ml-math/graph-theory/gnn-intro.subtitle: Neural networks that operate on graph-structured data. From social networks to molecules, GNNs learn representations that respect the relational structure of the world.

children.children: What is a graph neural network?

children: is a neural network that learns from data shaped as a graph, such as social networks, molecules or road maps. Each layer updates every node's vector by gathering messages from its neighbours and combining them with the node's own features, a step called
, so after several layers each node's embedding reflects its wider neighbourhood.

children.children: Traditional neural networks assume data comes in a fixed structure: images are grids of pixels, text is a sequence of tokens, audio is a 1D waveform. But much of the world's data is relational entities connected by relationships that form complex networks.

children: Social networks, molecules, transportation systems, knowledge graphs, protein interactions, citation networks: none of these fit neatly into grids or sequences. They are
: nodes connected by edges, with no fixed ordering or regular structure.
are a family of neural network architectures designed specifically for graph-structured data. They learn to transform and propagate information across the graph while respecting its topology.

children.children: Could you just flatten a graph into a feature vector and use a standard MLP? Technically yes, but you would lose critical information:
Graphs have variable sizes, no fixed input dimension
Node ordering is arbitrary, same graph, infinite permutations
Adjacency matrix is O(n²) and mostly zeros
Molecules as graphs. Predict toxicity, binding affinity, solubility from molecular structure.
Friend recommendations, bot detection, influence prediction, community detection.
User-item bipartite graphs. Pinterest, Uber Eats, Twitter all use GNNs.
Road networks as graphs. Google Maps uses GNNs for ETA prediction.
A GNN is a neural network that takes a graph as input and produces transformed representations. The key constraint: the network must respect the graph structure.

children: Each of the n nodes has a d-dimensional feature vector (e.g., atom type, user profile)
Which nodes are connected (or weighted/directed versions)

GCN vs GAT vs GraphSAGE: what is the difference?

The main GNN architectures differ in how they combine neighbour information. A GCN averages neighbours with fixed weights based on node degree, GAT learns attention weights so that more relevant neighbours count more, and GraphSAGE samples a fixed number of neighbours and aggregates them, which lets it produce embeddings for nodes it never saw during training.

/ml-math/graph-theory/message-passing.subtitle: The fundamental paradigm behind all modern GNN architectures. Understand this, and you understand GNNs.

children.children: What Is Message Passing in GNNs?

children: , we saw that GNNs learn by aggregating information from neighbors.
is the formal framework that unifies virtually all GNN architectures.

children.children: The idea is elegant: each node sends "messages" to its neighbors, collects messages from its neighbors, and uses them to update its own representation. Different GNN architectures (GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE, GIN) are just different implementations of this same idea.

children.className: bg-teal-100 dark:bg-teal-950/30 border-l-4 border-teal-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children: Message passing is a form of

. By forcing nodes to learn from their local neighborhoods, we inject the prior knowledge that "connected things are related." This is similar to how CNNs inject the prior that "nearby pixels are related."

children.children: The Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) framework, introduced by Gilmer et al. (2017), provides a unified view. One layer of message passing consists of three steps:

Combines all incoming messages (must be permutation-invariant: sum, mean, max, attention)
Merges aggregated message with node's current features (usually an MLP or GRU)

children.className: bg-indigo-100 dark:bg-indigo-950/30 border-l-4 border-indigo-500 p-5 rounded-r-lg

they implement MESSAGE, AGGREGATE, and UPDATE. This abstraction makes it easy to understand and compare different approaches.

/ml-math/information-theory/shannon-entr.subtitle: The mathematical measure of uncertainty, surprise, and information. The foundation of all information theory.

children: measures how unpredictable a random variable is: the average number of bits needed to encode its outcomes. It is
. A fair coin has 1 bit of entropy, a certain outcome has 0, and the uniform distribution has the most entropy for a given number of outcomes.
In 1948, Claude Shannon published "A Mathematical Theory of Communication," creating the field of Information Theory. He asked a deceptively simple question:

Before Shannon, "information" was vague and philosophical. After Shannon, information became a precise, measurable quantity, as fundamental as mass or energy. This single insight underlies everything from data compression (ZIP files) to neural networks (

children: (Kullback-Leibler divergence) measures how much a probability distribution P differs from a reference distribution Q. It is the expected number of extra bits, or nats, needed to encode samples from P with a code built for Q. It is never negative, is zero only when P equals Q, and is not symmetric.

children.children: In geometry, we measure distance between points with Euclidean distance. But how do we measure the "distance" between two probability distributions?

(Kullback-Leibler Divergence, also called Relative Entropy) quantifies this difference. It measures how much information is lost when we approximate one distribution with another.

children: is how much a split reduces entropy in a decision tree. It equals the entropy of the parent node minus the size-weighted average entropy of the child nodes. A decision tree computes it for every candidate feature and splits on the one with the highest gain, since that split makes the children purest.

ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3) uses Information Gain to build trees greedily:
Calculate H(S) for the current node.
For every possible feature A, calculate IG(S, A).
Split the data using that feature.
Recurse on each child until nodes are pure or max depth is reached.

ID3 only handles categorical features. Its successors C4.5 and CART split a numeric feature such as temperature with a threshold: sort the values, try a cut between each pair of neighbouring values, and keep the threshold with the highest gain. /ml-math/information-theory/perplexity.subtitle: The standard evaluation metric for language models. How confused is your model?

children: measures how well a language model predicts a text. It is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood of each actual next token, which is the same as the exponential of the cross-entropy loss. A perplexity of N means the model is as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among N tokens. Lower is better.

children.children: When you read "The cat sat on the ___", your brain instantly predicts words like "mat", "floor", or "couch". You are confident about what comes next. But for "I really want to ___", many words could follow: eat, sleep, dance, leave, scream. You are less certain.

children: measures exactly this: how "surprised" or "confused" a language model is when predicting the next word. It quantifies the model's uncertainty across an entire text.

children.className: bg-muted/50 border border-border rounded-lg p-5 mb-6

children: output probability distributions over thousands of possible next tokens. But how do we compare models? We need a single number that captures "how good are these predictions overall?"
We could use raw probability, but multiplying thousands of small probabilities gives tiny numbers like
. Perplexity converts this into an interpretable scale.
measures uncertainty in bits. Perplexity transforms entropy into "effective number of choices" by exponentiating:
. This gives us a more intuitive interpretation.

children.className: bg-purple-100 dark:bg-purple-950/30 border-l-4 border-purple-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg mb-6

children.children: Perplexity = "How many equally likely choices is the model effectively picking from?"

If a language model has perplexity 50, it is "as confused as if it had to choose uniformly among 50 options at each position." The model's complex probability distribution is equivalent to rolling a 50-sided die.
Lower perplexity = higher confidence = better predictions. A model that "knows" what comes next has low perplexity.

/ml-math/information-theory/jensen-shann.subtitle: A symmetric, smoothed version of KL Divergence. The metric that powers GANs.

children: is a powerful tool for measuring the difference between probability distributions. However, it has two fundamental limitations:
KL(P||Q) is not equal to KL(Q||P). The "direction" matters.
If P(x) > 0 but Q(x) = 0 for any x, KL divergence becomes infinite.
, introduced by Jianhua Lin in 1991, elegantly solves both problems. It measures how much each distribution diverges from their
, creating a symmetric and bounded measure.

children.className: bg-purple-100 dark:bg-purple-950/30 border-l-4 border-purple-500 p-6 rounded-r-lg

children.children: JSD is named after Johan Jensen (of Jensen's Inequality) and Claude Shannon (the father of information theory). It was designed to create a "smoothed" and symmetric version of KL divergence for practical applications.

children.className: bg-card border border-border rounded-lg p-4 mb-6 text-center

children.children: JSD is defined as the average KL divergence of P and Q from this mixture M:

children.className: bg-card border-2 border-purple-500 dark:border-purple-700 rounded-xl p-8 mb-6 text-center overflow-hidden

children.children: JSD(P \| Q) = \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}(P \| M) + \frac{1}{2} D_{KL}(Q \| M)

children.className: bg-purple-100 dark:bg-purple-950/30 border-l-4 border-purple-500 p-4 rounded-r-lg

children: Instead of directly comparing P to Q (which is asymmetric), we compare
P and Q to their "meeting point" M. This naturally creates symmetry.

children.children: JSD can be expressed in several equivalent ways, each providing different intuitions:

children.className: bg-card p-4 rounded text-center mb-3 overflow-x-auto

Where Z is a binary variable indicating whether a sample comes from P or Q. JSD equals the
between the sample and its source.

children.children: JSD equals zero only when the two distributions are identical at every point. This is a strict equality condition.

children: JSD is a sum of two KL divergences, both of which are non-negative. For the sum to be zero, both must be zero.
implies Q = M. Therefore P = Q = M.
KL Divergence can be zero in one direction but not the other if the supports differ. JSD's zero condition is cleaner and more intuitive.

children.children: JSD(\lambda P_1 + (1-\lambda)P_2 \| Q) \leq \lambda \cdot JSD(P_1 \| Q) + (1-\lambda) \cdot JSD(P_2 \| Q)
JSD is convex in both of its arguments. Mixing two distributions and then computing JSD gives a value no larger than the weighted average of individual JSDs.

children: Convexity guarantees that gradient-based methods won't get stuck in local minima when minimizing JSD. Any local minimum is also a global minimum.
This convexity is partly why the original GAN objective (which minimizes JSD) has nice theoretical properties, even though practical training can still be unstable due to the discriminator's role.

children.children: WGAN replaces JSD with the Wasserstein (Earth Mover's) distance. Unlike JSD, Wasserstein distance provides meaningful gradients even when distributions don't overlap. This led to more stable GAN training.

Drag the slider to separate the generator distribution from real data. Watch how JSD saturates and gradients vanish when distributions don't overlap, while Wasserstein distance maintains useful gradients.
